To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the net outcome (facilitation or competition) of biotic interactions depends on both stress tolerance and competitive-response ability of the interacting species, and that the relative stress tolerance and competitive response of a particular species determine the outcome of its biotic interactions.
the outcome of biotic in- teractions depends on the relative stress experienced by a species and its competitive-response ability.

(1) the net outcome of a biotic interaction depends on the relative stress of the interacting species and their competitive response ability, and (2) the relative stress of species is determined by the relative ecological optimum of the species.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the role of stress tolerance in determining the outcome of biotic inter- actions, and the importance of relative differences among species in stress tolerance in deter- mining the outcome of biotically induced stress.
the relative effects of abiotic stress and biotic interactions on species performance and the outcome of biotic interac- tions.
the relative importance of abiotic stress and biotic interactions in determining species distributions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the net outcome is determined by the interaction of the stress tolerance and competitive-response ability of the species.

facilitation and competition are not mutually exclusive processes and that the outcome of biotic interaction depends on both the abiotic stress level of a species and its competitive-response ability.
the relative importance of facilitation and competition in a community is determined by the relative importance of abiotic and biotic interactions for each of the species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
species differ in their fundamental niche optima, but the net outcome of interactions is relative to the intensity of abiotic stress experienced by each species in its natural habitat.
the net outcome depends on the relative stress tolerance and competitive response ability of a species.
the net outcome depends on both the abiotic conditions and on the species involved in the interaction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the outcome of biotic and abiotic interactions among plants is relative, and depends on the ecological context in which these interactions are studied.
the net outcome for a species is not a simple additive function of the effects of biotic interactions and abiotic stress, but rather depends on their relative importance.

the outcome of biotic inter- actions depends on how the relative stress experienced by the species in the field is translated into the relative competitive ability of the species in a particular biotic interaction.
